topic.title: The Tangent Function
topic.summary: The tangent function as the slope of the terminal ray, its period of π, its vertical asymptotes, its increasing and changing concavity between asymptotes, and its additive and multiplicative transformations.

lesson.title: The Tangent Function
lesson.summary: The tangent function as the slope of the terminal ray, its period of π, its vertical asymptotes, its increasing and changing concavity between asymptotes, and its additive and multiplicative transformations.
learningGoals: 3.8.A Construct representations of the tangent function using the unit circle.
3.8.B Describe key characteristics of the tangent function.
3.8.C Describe additive and multiplicative transformations involving the tangent function.
lesson.bigIdea: The tangent function gives the slope of the terminal ray. The slope repeats every half turn and does not exist when the ray is vertical, so tangent has period π and a vertical asymptote every π units.
lesson.context: Topic 3.2 defined the tangent of a single angle. This topic graphs it as a function and transforms it, using the same a, b, c, and d as the sinusoidal functions in Topic 3.6.

sections.title: 3.8.A · The tangent function gives the slope of the terminal ray.

blocks.text: Given an angle of measure θ in standard position and a unit circle centered at the origin, there is a point, P, where the terminal ray intersects the circle. The tangent function, f(θ) = tan θ, gives the slope of the terminal ray.

Because the slope of the terminal ray is the ratio of the change in the y-values to the change in the x-values between any two points on the ray, the tangent function is also the ratio of the sine function to the cosine function. Therefore, tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ), where cos θ ≠ 0.
Example: if sin θ = −3/5 and cos θ = 4/5, then tan θ = (−3/5)/(4/5) = −3/4. The terminal ray points down and to the right, so its slope is negative.

sections.takeaway: tan θ = slope of the terminal ray = sin θ/cos θ.

sections.title: 3.8.B · Period π, asymptotes where cos θ = 0, always increasing between them.
sections.conceptTitle: Period, asymptotes, and concavity of tangent

blocks.text: Because the slope values of the terminal ray repeat every one-half revolution of the circle, the tangent function has a period of π.
The tangent function demonstrates periodic asymptotic behavior at input values θ = π/2 + kπ, for integer values of k, because cos θ = 0 at those values.
The tangent function increases and its graph changes from concave down to concave up between consecutive asymptotes.

blocks.caption: y = tan θ with its vertical asymptotes at θ = ±π/2 and ±3π/2
blocks.alt: Repeating branches. Each branch rises from negative infinity near one dashed vertical asymptote to positive infinity near the next, passing through a zero at θ = −π, 0, and π, where it changes from concave down to concave up.

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: On −π/2 < θ < π/2, tan θ is increasing; its graph is concave down for −π/2 < θ < 0 and concave up for 0 < θ < π/2, so (0, 0) is a point of inflection.

sections.takeaway: Period π; asymptotes at π/2 + kπ; zeros and inflection points at kπ.

sections.title: 3.8.C · Transformations of tangent work like those of sine and cosine.

blocks.text: The graph of the additive transformation g(θ) = tan θ + d of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a vertical translation of the graph of f and the line containing its points of inflection by d units.
The graph of the additive transformation g(θ) = tan(θ + c) of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a horizontal translation, or phase shift, of the graph of f by −c units.

The graph of the multiplicative transformation g(θ) = a tan θ of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a vertical dilation of the graph of f by a factor of |a|. If a < 0, the transformation involves a reflection over the x-axis.

The graph of the multiplicative transformation g(θ) = tan(bθ) of the tangent function f(θ) = tan θ is a horizontal dilation of the graph of f and differs in period by a factor of |1/b|. If b < 0, the transformation involves a reflection over the y-axis.

The graph of y = f(θ) = a tan(b(θ + c)) + d is a vertical dilation of the graph of y = tan θ by a factor of |a|, has a period of |1/b|π units, is a vertical shift of the line containing the points of inflection of the graph of y = tan θ by d units, and is a phase shift of −c units.

blocks.caption: y = a tan(b(θ + c)) + d. Move the sliders to compare with y = tan θ (dashed).
blocks.alt: A tangent graph starting as y = 2 tan(θ/2) + 1, with period 2π and inflection points on the line y = 1, drawn over the dashed graph of y = tan θ. Sliders change a, b, c, and d.

blocks.text: Example: f(θ) = 3 tan(2θ) − 1 has period |1/2|π = π/2, and its points of inflection lie on y = −1. Its asymptotes are where 2θ = π/2 + kπ, that is, θ = π/4 + kπ/2.

sections.takeaway: Period π/|b|; no amplitude, because tangent is unbounded.

connections.title: Vertical asymptotes of quotients
connections.body: Topic 1.9 found vertical asymptotes of rational functions where the denominator is 0 and the numerator is not. tan θ = sin θ/cos θ has asymptotes for the same reason, wherever cos θ = 0.
connections.transferQuestion: Why is there no asymptote of tan θ at θ = π, where sin θ = 0?
connections.feedback: At θ = π the denominator cos θ = −1 is not 0, so tan π = 0 is a zero, not an asymptote.

connections.title: Undoing tangent
connections.body: Because tangent repeats every π, it has an inverse only on a restricted domain. Topic 3.9 restricts it to −π/2 < θ < π/2 to define the arctangent.
connections.transferQuestion: Which angle in −π/2 < θ < π/2 has tan θ = 1?

glossary.definition: The period of the function is the smallest positive value k such that f(x + k) = f(x) for all x in the domain. Consequently, the behavior of a periodic function is completely determined by any interval of width k.
In the coordinate plane, an angle is in standard position when the vertex coincides with the origin and one ray coincides with the positive x-axis. The other ray is called the terminal ray.

In the coordinate plane, an angle is in standard position when the vertex coincides with the origin and one ray coincides with the positive x-axis. The other ray is called the terminal ray. Positive and negative angle measures indicate rotations from the positive x-axis in the counterclockwise and clockwise direction, respectively. Angles in standard position that share a terminal ray differ by an integer number of revolutions.

The graph of the additive transformation g(θ) = sin(θ + c) of the sine function f(θ) = sin θ is a horizontal translation, or phase shift, of the graph of f by −c units. The same transformation of the cosine function yields the same result.
